01 / YOUR ENCOUNTERS

Start with your numbers

Count people, not times. Use the same time period for every field.

Some people were in both sex groups?

They count once as a partner, with acts in each group. Kissing is calculated separately.

“Protected” means a latex or synthetic condom. Birth control and withdrawal do not prevent STIs.

02 / PUT IT IN CONTEXT

Partner infection ≠ transmission

These models ask whether at least one partner might have an infection if partners matched the reference population. They do not estimate whether you acquired it.

WHO global reference prevalence: HSV-1 64% (any site), HSV-2 13%, and active syphilis 0.6%. These averages are illustrative, not your partners’ rates. Percentages are not your chance of infection and cannot be added together.

Assumes independent partners with identical prevalence. Real networks, age, location, infection site, symptoms, and treatment differ. Do not add these percentages together.

i
What changes with protection?

Condoms reduce transmission risk, but can leave skin exposed to herpes, HPV, or syphilis. This tab models a partner’s infection status only; the HIV tab models transmission.

Kissing & HIV

Saliva alone and closed-mouth kissing do not transmit HIV. Rare blood-contact situations are different. There is no dependable per-kiss HSV transmission percentage.

02 / A TRANSMISSION SCENARIO

Explore an HIV scenario

An educational model for someone initially HIV-negative. Choose assumptions first; this is not a personal diagnosis or validated clinical calculator.

Your assumption, not a sourced local rate. Overall HIV prevalence includes people who cannot sexually transmit HIV; do not substitute it directly.

The selected sex type applies to all acts. For a partner in both groups, both act counts apply. No PrEP or PEP is modeled; if used, this scenario does not represent your risk.

This HIV estimate is a scenario, not a diagnosis. Condom effects are approximate; individual circumstances can change risk. No uncertainty interval is calculated.

Condom figures are approximate. The model applies cohort risk reductions to per-act estimates. That is a modeling assumption, not a directly measured per-act condom effect. Anal-sex reductions come from studies of men who have sex with men; applicability to other populations is uncertain. Viral load, acute infection, other STIs, and individual circumstances can change risk.
Show the math & assumptions

For each distinct partner: t = q × [1 − (1 − rᵤ)ᵃ × (1 − r꜀)ᵇ]. Then across partners: P = 1 − ∏(1 − t).

q is the assumed chance of transmissible HIV, sampled once per partner; a and b are condomless and condom acts. Repeated acts share the partner’s infection status. Acts are conditionally independent with fixed risk; partner statuses are independent.

CDC reference risks per 10,000 condomless acts: vaginal insertive 4, vaginal receptive 8, anal insertive 11, anal receptive 138. The condom multiplier uses reductions of 80%, 80%, 63%, and 72%, respectively. The 72% figure is one cohort estimate; another study found 91% per partnership. They are different measures, not confidence bounds. These older studies remain on CDC’s current reference page. No uncertainty interval is calculated. Read CDC’s evidence ↗

Real figures. Visible limitations.

What this app can calculate

01

Partner-status scenarios. For each infection separately, 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ, using WHO reference prevalence p and distinct partners n. Global averages are illustrative, not estimates for your actual partners. Kissing and sex groups stay separate.

02

An HIV acquisition scenario. Using CDC exposure estimates, a sex type, act counts, and explicit partner-status assumptions. Condom effects are approximated. Maintained viral suppression prevents sexual HIV transmission (U=U).

03

What remains unknown. A personal “any STI” probability, a per-kiss risk, and reliable individual transmission percentages for HPV, herpes, syphilis, chlamydia, or gonorrhea cannot be calculated from these counts. No combined score is produced.

THE USEFUL NEXT STEP

Let testing answer the personal question.

Many STIs have no symptoms. A clinician can advise on tests, timing, and throat or rectal swabs where relevant. A recent negative test may need repeating after its window period.
